extraction.name: PIQA
extraction.description: A benchmark dataset for physical commonsense reasoning that tests natural language understanding models' ability to answer questions about everyday physical situations and object manipulation. The dataset focuses on everyday situations with atypical solutions, inspired by instructables.com.
extraction.creator: Yonatan Bisk, Rowan Zellers, Ronan Le Bras, Jianfeng Gao, Yejin Choi
extraction.publisher: Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Data was collected through crowdsourced annotations using instructables.com as inspiration. Annotators were prompted with links to instructables and asked to construct goal-solution pairs by extracting or being inspired by component tasks from the instructions. They articulated physical goals (often centered on atypical materials) and provided both valid solutions and invalid permutations of those solutions.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data source was instructables.com, a crowdsourced collection of instructions for various tasks from cooking to car repair. Users on instructables provide images or videos detailing each step and lists of required tools. These instructables served as prompts to inspire annotators to create goal-solution pairs.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators were provided with instructables.com links as inspiration and asked to: 1) articulate a physical goal, 2) provide a valid solution, and 3) create a 'trick' - a subtly incorrect solution that sounds reasonable but is wrong due to misunderstanding of preconditions or physics. Examples with low agreement during validation were removed. Annotators had to pass a qualification HIT (>80% accuracy) identifying well-formed goal-solution pairs before participating in the main annotation task.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Data was collected in batches and validated by other annotators for correctness. Users with low agreement were disqualified. Examples with low agreement were removed from the dataset. AFLite algorithm was used to remove stylistic artifacts and trivial examples.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Multiple annotations per item during validation phase
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: AFLite algorithm for removing annotation artifacts, BERT-Large for computing embeddings to identify biased instances, Spacy for tokenization
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset has some limitations including that manual inspection shows some model 'mistakes' are actually correct but required a web-search to verify. The dataset was constructed to be adversarial to BERT. Some examples are truncated at 150 tokens which affects 1% of the data.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The work aims to advance AI systems' understanding of physical commonsense knowledge, which is critical for day-to-day human life and for developing robots that interact with the world and understand natural language. The authors emphasize that knowledge should be learned from interaction with the world to eventually be communicated with language.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is designed to evaluate language representations on their knowledge of physical commonsense and to probe the inner workings of deep pretrained language models. It serves as a diagnostic for physical understanding and a benchmark for testing natural language understanding systems on physical commonsense reasoning tasks.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Dataset construction used adversarial filtering to handle spurious biases. Training, development, and test folds were automatically produced by AFLite (Adversarial Filtering Lite). Examples were truncated at 150 tokens, which affects 1% of the data.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Text preprocessing included tokenization and lowercasing with punctuation removal for edit distance computation. Examples were truncated at 150 tokens using the transformers library.
